fetched_contents.text: Internal limiting membrane peeling with different dyes in the surgery of idiopathic macular hole: a systematic review of literature and network Meta-analysis Abstract AIM To evaluate the effect of internal limiting membrane (ILM) peeling with indocyanine green (ICG), brilliant blue G (BBG), triamcinolone acetonide (TA), trypan blue (TB), or without dye for the treatment of idiopathic macular hole (IMH). METHODS A search was conducted using PubMed, EMBASE, and CENTRAL (Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials) for related studies published before October 2018. RESULTS A total of 29 studies and 2514 eyes were included in this network Meta-analysis. For IMH closure, the rank from the best to the worse treatment was: BBG, TB, TA, ICG, and no dye. There was a significant difference in postoperative IMH closure rate between BBG and no dye. The rank of the best to the worse treatment to improve visual acuity was: BBG, TB, no dye, TA, and ICG. The improvement rate of visual acuity after using BBG was significantly higher than ICG. The improvement rate of visual acuity was more favorable with TB than ICG, TA, and no dye. CONCLUSION BBG can contribute to better anatomical and functional outcomes compared to other dyes for ILM peeling in patients with IMH. The results show that the best treatment of ILM peeling with dyes is BBG. Keywords: idiopathic macular hole, brilliant blue G, trypan blue, internal limiting membrane peeling, network Meta-analysis INTRODUCTION Idiopathic macular hole (IMH) is an important condition that leads to blindness[1]. Patients with IMH have a prevalence of 8 cases per 100 000 people[2], and patients with visual impairment have an incidence of 0.2/1000 to 0.3/1000[3]–[4]. IMH has a serious impact on patients' quality of life, however, it can be repaired by the surgery of pars plana vitrectomy (PPV)[5]. In 1971, Machemer et al[6] firstly described a vitrectomy. With the development of medical technology, vitrectomy combined with inner limiting membrane (ILM) peeling shows better outcomes compared to no ILM peeling[7]–[9]. However, the ILM is thin and transparent which makes it a challenge for the surgeon, and it is difficult to distinguish the boundary and range of the peeling[10]. It is for this reason that indocyanine green (ICG) dye, which was initially used for fluorescein angiography, was firstly used for ILM staining in 2000 and improved the visualization of ILM during the surgery and promoted the development of ILM peeling[11]. Since then, ILM peeling with ICG has been widely reported to promote the surgery of MHs[12]–[13]. However, ICG could also cause damage to the retinal ganglion cells and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) because of its toxicity, the mechanism might be related to the oxidative toxicity of ICG[14]. Brilliant blue G (BBG) is an alternative dye for staining ILM and has been frequently used throughout the world. However, in vitro, it has been shown that BBG is related to cellular toxicity[14]–[15], and other dyes applied to ILM peeling surgeries have also shown toxic effects on the retina[16]–[17], such as trypan blue (TB) and triamcinolone acetonide (TA)[2],[18]. In summary, almost all kinds of biological dyes have potential side effects on the retina. At present, there are few comparative reports of postoperative results from ICG, BBG, TB, TA, and no dye assisted ILM peeling for patients with IMH. Therefore, this network Meta-analysis study is mainly for patients with IMH, to analysis and summarize the anatomical outcome (rate of postoperative primary MH closure) and functional outcome [rate of vision improvement and best corrected visual acuity (BCVA)] for ILM peeling with ICG, BBG, TB, TA, and no dye. MATERIALS AND METHODS This systematic review and a Meta-analysis were conducted according to the recommendations from the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Review of Interventions[19]. Search Strategy The PubMed, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CENTRAL (Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials) were searched for related published studies, with no language restrictions before October 2018. The terms used for the systematic search were (“brilliant blue”, OR “indocyanine green”, OR “triamcinolone acetonide”, OR “trypan blue”, OR ICG, OR TB, OR TA, OR BBG) AND (“internal limiting membrane peeling”, OR “primary macular hole”, OR “idiopathic macular hole”). We also manually collected the reference lists for the original studies and review articles were examined by internet-based search for additional eligible articles. Eligibility Criteria The articles taken from the internet-based search were established to screen the qualified trials. The eligible studies must have been met: 1) comparative studies; 2) contained at least two groups, with the ILM-peeling procedure and with application of ICG, or BBG, or TB, or TA, or peeling without staining; 3) included only IMH patients, and ILM peeling was conducted in case and control groups; 4) at least one of the outcomes of interest was included. Data Extraction and Quality Assessment The data were extracted independently by two reviewers and were rechecked after the first extraction. Any disagreement of eligibility during the extraction was discussed by the two reviewers and resolved. The extracted information from each study included the first author, year, study type, number of subjects, age, stages of MHs, preoperative BCVAs (logarithm of the minimal angle of resolution, logMAR), follow-up time, and dyes. The outcomes of interest were extracted and included the following: the primary closure rate (MH closure after the initial surgery) and the number of people with improved visual acuity. We contacted the authors for any missing data. The quality of the retrospective studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS)[20]. fetched_contents.text: Brilliant blue G-assisted peeling of the internal limiting membrane in macular hole surgery Abstract Dye-assisted internal limiting membrane (ILM) peeling and gas tamponade is the surgery of choice for idiopathic macular holes. Indocyanine green and trypan blue have been extensively used to stain the ILM. However, the retinal toxicity of indocyanine green and non-uniform staining with trypan blue has necessitated development of newer vital dyes. Brilliant blue G has recently been introduced as one such dye with adequate ILM staining and no reported retinal toxicity. We performed a 23-gauge pars plana vitrectomy with brilliant blue G-assisted ILM peeling in six patients with idiopathic macular holes, to assess the staining characteristics and short-term adverse effects of this dye. Adequate staining assisted in the complete removal of ILM and closure of macular holes in all cases. There was no evidence of intraoperative or postoperative dye-related toxicity. Brilliant blue G appears to be safe dye for ILM staining in macular hole surgery. Keywords: Brilliant blue G, macular hole, internal limiting membrane, peeling ---------------------------------------- Internal limiting membrane (ILM) peeling, one of the most challenging procedures in vitreoretinal surgery, has been made easier with selective staining of this optically clear tissue with a number of vital dyes.[1] Indocyanine green (ICG) was one of the first dyes used for ILM peeling.[2] However, its use has recently declined due to an increasing number of reports of its toxic effect on the retina.[3,4] Trypan blue appears to be safe for intraocular use, but it stains the ILM to a lesser degree.[5] In recent times, brilliant blue G (BBG) has been introduced as an alternative to stain the ILM and appears to have no retinal toxicity in humans.[6–8] In the present study, we have investigated the efficacy and short-term safety of BBG-assisted ILM peeling in macular hole surgery. Materials and Methods After approval by the local institutional review board and ethics committee, six eyes of six patients [Table 1] with idiopathic macular holes were included in this prospective, interventional, non-comparative clinical case series. All the patients underwent a complete ophthalmic clinical examination including best corrected visual acuity (BCVA), applanation intraocular pressure, Goldmann visual fields, color and red free photographs, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) (Stratus OCT III, Carl Zeiss Meditech Inc, Jena, Germany) preoperatively, and every four weeks after surgery, for a period of 20 weeks. All the patients underwent 23-gauge three port pars plana vitrectomy (Alcon Inc., Fort Worth, Texas. USA). BBG solution (Fluoron GmbH, Neu-Ulm, Germany) was injected over the macular area and washed out after about 30 seconds. ILM staining was noted intraoperatively as good, faint or absent. The stained ILM was then peeled [Fig. 1a] with the use of an end gripping forceps. Gas fluid exchange was performed with 20% sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) mixture and the patients were advised prone position for one week. Table 1. Baseline and follow-up clinical characteristics of all patients Case Age / Gender Macular hole stage Preoperative BCVA BCVA at 20 weeks, postoperatively Lens status Postoperative macular hole status 1 60/F 3 0.15 0.40 Phakic Closed 2 65/F 4 0.07 0.10 Phakic Closed 3 62/M 3 0.15 0.40 Pseudophakic Closed 4 70/F 4 0.10 0.10 Pseudophhakic Closed 5 68/M 4 0.07 0.15 Pseudophakic Closed 6 63/F 4 0.10 0.25 Phakic Closed Statistical analysis of pre- and postoperative BCVA was performed using the two-tailed Wilcoxon signed ranks test. Differences were considered significant when P < 0.05. Results Four women and two men with a mean age of 64.6 years were included in the study. All patients were followed-up for 20 weeks postoperatively. All macular holes were completely closed in all patients in the first visit (one week) and remained closed at all subsequent four-weekly visits [Fig. 1b and c]. The mean visual acuity improved statistically and significantly from 0.11 preoperatively to 0.23 at the last follow-up postoperatively (P = 0.0325). Staining of the ILM was good in all cases and allowed for an easy and atraumatic removal of the ILM. The complete data on our patients is given in Table 1. We did not observe any visual field defects in any of the patients that might have been caused by dye toxicity. There was no evidence of any retinal pigment epithelium abnormality or nerve fiber layer defect seen in the red-free photographs during any of the postoperative visits of all patients. Despite the 85% to 95% anatomical closure rate, several aspects of the procedure are well accepted whereas some may remain controversial among vitreoretinal surgeons. An international panel of experts (IPE) comprising 27 experts from 10 countries/territories was established to evaluate a total of 38 consensus statements on ILM peeling extent, vital dye selection, face-down positioning requirements, tamponade options, timing of surgery and re-surgery, management of difficult and refractory cases, and adjuvant therapies. The objective is to synthesize evidence-based real-world practice recommendations from leading global experts to guide the management of FTMH. Of the 38 statements, the IPE reached consensus (75% voted as “Strong Agreement” or “Agreement”) on 29 (76.3%). The IPE emphasized the importance of individualized patient factors—such as hole size, chronicity, lens status, and preoperative visual acuity—in surgical planning and tempering patient’s postoperative expectations. There was strong agreement on the need of adequate peeling of the ILM, adjunctive measures including the inverted ILM flap, and face-down positioning for large and refractory FTMH. Controversial statements, such as the use of air tamponade or observation of small FTMH, not reaching consensus are identified. We hope the consensus statements agreed and disagreed by the IPE would help serve as good reference and guidelines in managing FTMH. The classification of macular holes (MHs) by size is crucial in determining surgical options and predicting outcomes notably since size serves as a prognostic factor. FTMHs are generally classified into three primary categories based on their minimum diameter: small (< 250 μm), medium (250 to 400 μm), and large (> 400 μm) [1]. This classification allows surgeons to tailor the management approach depending on the size and associated characteristics of the MH [1]. Literature suggests that small MHs have higher spontaneous closure rates than larger ones. Non-surgical MH closure using enzymatic vitreolysis has shown to be successful in small MHs [5]. It remains Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved for use in MH less than 400 μm but its use has declined over the years due to lower success rates compared to conventional vitrectomy and potential adverse effects like troublesome floaters, photopsia, transient blurring of vision, and pain [7]. This indicates that BBG is generally the most effective dye for both anatomical closure and visual outcomes, while ICG is the least effective among the dyes studied.

For complete ILM peeling and MH closure, the evidence is mixed in the provided material. The meta-analysis reports better closure rates with dyes than without, but the provided excerpts do not specify whether every dye consistently achieves complete ILM peeling or whether some dyes are more difficult to remove [N1-F1]. The BBG study, by contrast, reports that staining was adequate in all cases and that complete ILM removal and MH closure occurred in all six patients [N3-F2]. This suggests that BBG may be especially effective for achieving complete peeling and closure, while ICG and TB appear to be less consistently effective in the provided direct evidence [N1-F1].

Recurrence rates and long-term visual outcomes are less clearly quantified in the evidence here. The network meta-analysis provides closure rates and visual acuity improvement, but the provided excerpts do not explicitly report recurrence rates after closure [N1-F1]. ## Integrated final synthesis: how different intraoperative dyes compare in effectiveness and safety for ILM peeling in macular hole surgery

The evidence across the branch reports consistently supports the same broad conclusion: **dye-assisted ILM peeling improves macular hole closure compared to no dye, but the relative ranking of dyes differs by effectiveness, safety, and staining characteristics**. Among the most commonly reported dyes in MH surgery, **brilliant blue G (BBG), indocyanine green (ICG), trypan blue (TB), and triamcinolone acetonide (TA)** are the most frequently studied, with BBG and ICG appearing most prominently in direct comparisons [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-F2]. The evidence is strongest for BBG and weakest for ICG in the provided excerpts, but the overall ranking is supported by a systematic review and network meta-analysis [N1-F1].

---

## 1) Which dyes are most commonly used and how they differ

The most commonly reported dyes in MH surgery studies are **BBG, ICG, TB, and TA**. BBG and ICG are especially prominent in the direct comparison literature, while TB and TA are also common but less central in the provided evidence set [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-F2]. The consensus statement also notes that minimizing dye contact time to about 30 seconds to 1 minute is recommended, indicating that dye selection is often tied to protocol design rather than a single “best” dye [N5-F3].

### Dose, concentration, and application protocol differences
The evidence includes explicit concentration and application details for BBG. One study used **0.25 mg/mL BBG**, injected over the macular area, and washed out after about **30 seconds** [N3-F2]. The consensus statement reinforces the importance of minimizing contact time, suggesting that staining intensity and safety are both protocol-dependent [N5-F3]. The provided evidence does not give detailed concentrations for ICG or TB, but the BBG study’s protocol highlights that staining can vary as **good, faint, or absent** intraoperatively [N3-F2]. This implies that the same dye can be used with different concentrations and contact times, and that shorter contact time is advised as a safety measure [N5-F3].

### Dye-specific advantages and limitations for ILM visualization
BBG appears to offer the best balance of **adequate ILM staining** and **ease of use**. The BBG study reports good staining in all cases, allowing easy and atraumatic ILM removal, and concludes that BBG appears to be a safe dye for ILM staining in macular hole surgery [N3-F2]. ICG is noted as the first dye used for ILM staining and as improving visualization, but it is also linked to **retinal toxicity** and is associated with less favorable visual outcomes compared to BBG [N1-F1][N3-F2]. TB is described as **safer intraocularly than ICG**, but it stains the ILM to a lesser degree than ICG [N3-F2]. TA is mentioned in the network meta-analysis but is not detailed as extensively in the provided excerpts [N1-F1]. The consensus guidance also emphasizes minimizing contact time, suggesting that all dyes require careful protocol adjustment to balance staining adequacy with safety [N5-F3].

---

## 2) Effectiveness and outcomes associated with each dye

### Effectiveness for complete ILM peeling and macular hole closure
The evidence suggests that **dye-assisted ILM peeling improves MH closure compared to no dye**, but the relative effectiveness varies across dyes. The network meta-analysis ranks the treatments from best to worst for postoperative IMH closure as: **BBG, TB, TA, ICG, and no dye**, with a significant difference between BBG and no dye [N1-F1]. For visual acuity improvement, the ranking is: **BBG, TB, no dye, TA, and ICG**, with BBG showing a significantly higher improvement rate than ICG, and TB also more favorable than ICG and TA [N1-F1]. This indicates that **BBG is the most effective dye for both closure and visual outcomes**, while **ICG is the least effective** among the dyes studied [N1-F1].

The BBG study itself supports this conclusion by reporting **complete ILM removal and MH closure in all six patients** [N3-F2]. This suggests that BBG may be especially effective for achieving complete peeling and closure, while ICG and TB appear to be less consistently effective in the provided direct evidence [N1-F1]. The broader evidence on MH surgery notes that ILM peeling improves closure rates and reduces reoperation rates, but the provided excerpts do not isolate recurrence rates for each dye [N4-R3]. As a result, the evidence supports improved anatomical outcomes with dyes, but the long-term recurrence literature is thinner in the provided material [N1-F1][N4-R3].

### Recurrence rates and long-term visual outcomes
The provided evidence is **less clear on recurrence rates and long-term visual outcomes**. The network meta-analysis provides closure rates and visual acuity improvement, but it does not explicitly report recurrence rates after closure [N1-F1]. The BBG study reports short-term improvement in visual acuity, with preoperative BCVA improving from 0.11 to 0.23 at the last follow-up, but it does not provide long-term recurrence data [N3-F2]. Therefore, while the evidence supports improved anatomical outcomes with dyes, the long-term recurrence literature is not robust enough to draw a definitive conclusion from the provided material [N1-F1][N3-F2].

### Study quality and consistency across trials
The evidence base is heterogeneous but appears strongest for BBG and weakest for ICG in the provided excerpts. The network meta-analysis is the strongest direct comparison, but it includes 29 studies and 2514 eyes and is described as a systematic review and network meta-analysis conducted with Cochrane methods [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that “almost all kinds of biological dyes have potential side effects on the retina” and that comparative postoperative results are “few” for ICG, BBG, TB, TA, and no dye [N1-F1]. This suggests that the relative ranking may be influenced by the limited number of direct comparisons rather than a fully converged consensus. The provided evidence is therefore consistent enough to rank BBG as superior, but not so strong that every dye’s position is definitively settled [N1-F1].

---

## 3) Safety, toxicity, and complications

### Reported intraoperative and postoperative adverse events
The safety evidence is mixed but overall more favorable for BBG than for ICG and TB. The BBG study reports **no ocular or systemic side effects, no visual field defects, no retinal pigment epithelium abnormality, and no nerve fiber layer defect** during postoperative visits [N3-F2]. It concludes that BBG appears to be a safe dye for ILM staining in macular hole surgery [N3-F2]. The broader evidence on macular peeling notes that complications may include **retinal hemorrhages, retinoschisis, edema, paracentral scotomas, and electroretinogram (ERG) changes** [N3-R4]. The evidence also reports rare complications such as **choroidal neovascularization or retinal angiomatosis proliferation after ILM peeling**, likely secondary to trauma [N4-R5]. This implies that while BBG appears safer in the direct evidence, other complications are still associated with ILM peeling more generally and are not necessarily confined to one dye [N3-R4][N4-R5].

### Toxicity mechanisms and evidence for retinal damage or toxicity
The evidence points to multiple possible toxicity mechanisms. The network meta-analysis excerpt notes that ICG toxicity may be related to **oxidative toxicity**, while a post-market surveillance study cited in the evidence addresses **presumed phototoxicity from BBG and TB** [N1-F1][N6-R4]. The BBG study also discusses **photosensitizing properties of ICG** and **direct Müller cell damage during ICG-assisted ILM peeling**, while noting that BBG staining may reduce mechanical retinal trauma compared to ICG [N3-F2]. This suggests that toxicity may arise from both **direct dye effects** and **mechanical injury during peeling**, with ICG appearing to carry the strongest mechanistic concern [N3-F2].

### Which dyes appear safest and under what conditions
Based on the provided evidence, **BBG appears safest** in the direct evidence, especially when contact time is minimized and staining is adequate without excessive exposure [N3-F2][N5-F3]. **ICG is the most toxic** in the evidence, with reports of retinal toxicity, oxidative toxicity, and direct Müller cell damage, and it is ranked worse than BBG in both closure and visual outcomes [N1-F1][N3-F2]. **TB is safer intraocularly than ICG**, but it stains the ILM to a lesser degree and is not as strongly supported as BBG in the provided evidence [N3-F2]. The evidence also supports minimizing contact time as a safety strategy, implying that even “safe” dyes can become harmful if used excessively [N5-F3].

## 4) Newer evidence and missing dye comparisons

### Evidence gaps for newer or less-studied dyes
The provided evidence indicates that the literature is still evolving, and the evidence base remains incomplete. The network meta-analysis and direct comparisons in the provided evidence focus on BBG, ICG, TB, TA, and no dye, but they do not include newer dyes such as **Brilliant Blue G variants, other newer chromophores, or alternative staining protocols** in sufficient detail [N1-F1]. The evidence also does not provide a direct comparison for newer dyes such as BBG in complicated cases, although one source mentions its use at **0.25 mg/mL in complicated cases such as retinal detachment due to high myopic macular hole** [N6-R2]. This implies that newer evidence exists, but it is not fully represented in the provided excerpts and is still limited in scope [N1-F1][N6-R2].

### Recently reported staining protocols or safety warnings
Newer evidence includes **post-market surveillance and newer staining protocols**. The BBG study explicitly reports a protocol of injecting BBG over the macular area and washing it out after about **30 seconds**, while the consensus statement recommends minimizing dye contact time to approximately **30 seconds to 1 minute** [N3-F2][N5-F3]. Another source notes that **heavy trypan blue** eliminates the need for an air-fluid exchange and appears to have little retinal toxicity [N6-R3]. These newer protocol details suggest that staining practices have evolved, but they are not universally standardized in the provided evidence [N3-F2][N5-F3][N6-R3].

### How newer evidence changes the relative ranking of dyes
The newer evidence reinforces BBG’s safety profile while also introducing **phototoxicity concerns**, which may temper its apparent superiority [N3-F2][N6-R4]. The evidence also suggests that TB is safer intraocularly than ICG, but less effective for ILM staining than ICG, and that newer protocols can reduce contact time and potentially reduce toxicity [N3-F2][N5-F3][N6-R3]. Overall, the newer evidence supports the same general ranking of **BBG as the most favorable dye**, but it adds caution that even newer protocols and safety warnings do not eliminate toxicity concerns [N6-R4][N5-F3]. The main gap is that the provided evidence does not fully compare all newer or less-studied dyes, so the relative ranking should be interpreted as **partially updated but still incomplete** [N1-F1][N6-R4].

---

## 5) Bottom line: how to compare the dyes

If you want a practical ranking based on the evidence provided, the best-supported order is:

1. **BBG** – most effective for both closure and visual acuity, safest in the direct evidence, and easiest to use with adequate staining [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-F3].
2. **TB** – safer intraocularly than ICG, but less effective for ILM staining than ICG [N3-F2].
3. **TA** – less frequently detailed in the provided evidence, but still a dye used in MH surgery [N1-F1].
4. **ICG** – most toxic in the evidence, associated with oxidative toxicity and direct Müller cell damage, and ranked worse than BBG in both closure and visual outcomes [N1-F1][N3-F2].
5. **No dye** – used as a control, but less effective than dyes in the provided evidence [N1-F1].

### Practical guidance
The consensus statement and direct evidence both support minimizing **dye contact time** to about **30 seconds to 1 minute** to balance staining adequacy with safety [N5-F3]. For BBG, the evidence also supports a **0.25 mg/mL concentration** injected over the macular area and washed out after about **30 seconds** [N3-F2]. For TB, the evidence suggests it may be safer than ICG but less effective for ILM staining [N3-F2]. The newer evidence also highlights **phototoxicity concerns** for BBG and TB, so ongoing surveillance remains important [N6-R4].

### Final judgment
The evidence supports **BBG as the preferred dye** for ILM peeling in macular hole surgery, especially because it appears safest and most effective in the provided material [N1-F1][N3-F2]. However, the evidence base is **not fully converged**, and ICG remains the most toxic dye in the direct evidence [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The ranking should therefore be interpreted cautiously, with BBG favored for safety and effectiveness, ICG favored for historical visualization but with higher toxicity, and TB as a safer alternative with less staining intensity [N3-F2][N5-F3].
